sources.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

sources.title: Vestibular influence on auditory metrical interpretation
Fourteen-month-old infants use interpersonal synchrony as a cue to direct helpfulness
sources.authors: Cirelli LK, Wan SJ, Trainor LJ.
sources.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences

sources.title: Precursors of dancing and singing to music in three- to four-months-old infants
sources.authors: Fujii S, Watanabe H, Oohashi H, Hirashima M, Nozaki D, Taga G.

findings.finding: Infants engage in significantly more rhythmic movement when exposed to music and rhythmically regular sounds compared to speech.
findings.quote: infants engage in significantly more rhythmic movement to music and other rhythmically regular sounds than to speech

findings.finding: The degree of rhythmic coordination with music is positively related to how much positive affect infants display.
findings.quote: the degree of rhythmic coordination with music is positively related to displays of positive affect

findings.finding: Moving the body in time with a rhythm can bias and shape how auditory meters are perceived and interpreted.
findings.quote: moving the body on a certain beat--adults, by actively bouncing themselves in synchrony with the experimenter, and babies, by being bounced passively in the experimenter's arms--can bias their auditory metrical representation

findings.finding: Synchronous bouncing with another person acts as a direct social cue that encourages helpfulness and prosocial behavior.
findings.quote: Infants were significantly more likely to display helpfulness towards an adult experimenter following synchronous bouncing compared with asynchronous bouncing to music.

principle: Infants exhibit an innate predisposition for rhythmic movement and motor coordination in response to music, which is strongly linked to positive affect and physical motion.
for_the_teacher: Incorporate full-body bouncing or vestibular motion early in the lesson to help learners physically feel and interpret the musical beat.
